seoDescription: Learn the fundamentals of creating and editing pages in your WordPress dashboard. This tutorial guides you through the process of adding a new page, such as an 'About Us' page, from scratch. Discover the power of the WordPress block editor (Gutenberg) to add and arrange various types of content. We'll demonstrate how to use essential blocks like paragraphs, pullquotes, columns for side-by-side images, and separators to structure your page layout effectively for a professional, custom look.

summary:
## Getting Started with WordPress Pages

- Navigate to the **Pages** section in the left-hand menu of your WordPress dashboard to see a list of all current pages.
- Use the **search bar** in the top right to quickly find a specific page by keyword.
- Hover over any page title to access management options: **Edit**, **Quick Edit**, **Trash**, and **View**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pages are different from Posts.**
> - **Pages** are for static, timeless content like an "About Us" or "Contact" page.
> - **Posts** are for dynamic, chronological content like blog entries, which are displayed newest first.

## The WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg)

The block editor is the default way to create and edit pages in modern WordPress. It allows you to build your page piece by piece using content "blocks."

- To create a new page, click the **Add New** button at the top of the Pages section.
- The first step is to **Add title** for your page.
- Click the **`+` icon** to add a new block for text, images, or other elements.
- You can **Browse all** to see a full list of available blocks in a side panel.

## Key Blocks Demonstrated

- **Pullquote**: Creates a visually distinct quote to highlight important text.
- **Columns**: Allows you to create layouts with multiple columns (e.g., 50/50, 30/70), perfect for placing content side-by-side.
- **Image**: Used to upload a new image, select one from your Media Library, or insert one from a URL. Images can have captions added.
- **Separator**: Adds a horizontal line to visually divide sections of your page. Its style can be changed to a solid line, wide line, or dots.
- **Paragraph**: The most common block, used for standard body text.

> [!TIP]
> Blocks are easy to manage. You can **duplicate** an existing block to reuse its content or styling, and use the **up/down arrows** to quickly move blocks and reorder your page content.

## Page Management & Publishing

- Individual blocks have a **toolbar** for specific settings like alignment (left, right, center, full-width) and text formatting (bold, italic, links).

> [!NOTE]
> Before your page goes live, you will be prompted to review publishing settings.
> - **Visibility**: Set your page to Public, Private, or Password Protected.
> - **Publish**: You can publish immediately or schedule the page to go live at a future date and time.

- Always remember to either **Publish** your page to make it live or **Save draft** to save your progress without publishing it.
transcription:
## Introduction to Building a WordPress Page

Hey everyone, it is Josh here with HostGator. Today, we are excited to show you how to build a new WordPress website from the ground up.

In this series, we'll help you take your website from looking like this to looking like this, in just a few easy steps. Today, we're going to focus on how to create and edit a new page inside of your WordPress dashboard. And we'll show you how to edit an existing one, to add content for your visitors to see.

If you need to get caught up in this series, I've got links to them in the description below, but if not, let's get started.

## Navigating the WordPress Pages Dashboard

Now, we're kicking things off once again, inside of our WordPress dashboard. This time on the left-hand side, we're going to find the pages icon, and click there.

This takes us to our pages section inside the WordPress dashboard. As you can see all the pages that we have for our site are currently listed here. There's not too many since we just got started building, but these can add up very quickly. Be sure to note on the top right-hand corner, there's a search bar where you can easily search using keywords for any of the pages that you have.

## Understanding the Difference Between Pages and Posts

Before we get started on creating and editing any content, it's really good to note the difference between a page and a blog post. Blog posts are essentially blog-like content that's listed in reverse chronological order with the newest content at the top. These posts are usually present on your blog page, and we'll talk about that in a completely separate video.

Pages, however, are static content, such as your About Us, your Privacy Policy and your Contact Us pages. These are generally in a place where your content, like images, texts, blogs, posts, videos, and more can be displayed. Pages are individualized, and you can add as many and link to them as much as you want.

I know that I want an About Us page for this site. It looks like the one that comes default with this WordPress theme magically disappeared. I wonder how that happened.

## Page Management Options: Edit, Trash, and View

Now that we know what we're working with, let's take a look at some of the options that we have within the pages section to actually modify content. Let's hover over one of the existing pages here, and I'll show you some of the options that we have. I can hover over the Contact page here. We can see that we have an edit, a quick edit, a trash, and a view.

The edit button is going to be the best way to physically edit the content of your site. There's a quick edit option, but that really just deals with the date, slug, title, and a few other key details. The trash is exactly what it sounds like. If you want to delete the page, that's exactly how you do it, and view is if you want to see how the page actually looks.

Now that we've seen some of the options, let's take a look at the pages that I actually have. We've got my blog page, which is my post page, so any blog posts that I make will automatically show up there. I've got my contact page, privacy policy page, a sample page, and my front page, which is the one that comes default with the WordPress 2020 theme.

## Creating a New Page and Adding a Title

We'll move into editing shortly, but first, let's learn how to create a brand-new page. In the top left-hand corner, there's a button that says add new.

Welcome to the WordPress page editor. Now there's a new block editor in WordPress this year. If you need a tutorial on that, you can go ahead and click the next option down here. I'm going to show you a few things about the block editor too. We'll go ahead and exit out of this.

This is going to be my about us page, so the first thing I want to do is add the title. We'll click here under add title and we'll type about.

## Adding Your First Block: The Pullquote

Below the title, we'll have the option to either start adding text or choosing a new block. I want to show you a little bit about blocks because they're one of my favorite parts of WordPress. Let's click here and click the plus sign.

A little while ago, WordPress started to get really good with their built-in page editor. I love the block feature. Once we click on the plus sign, you can see that this navigation bar opens up to have a ton of different blocks available. What I'm going to do now is choose a block that's right for me.

As you can see, we've got paragraph, image, pullquote, gallery, heading. There's a ton of options here, and we're going to go over a lot of them. The first one I want to do is some really bold text. I'm going to choose pullquote.

Now that I clicked pullquote, I've got the option to either start adding text manually, or I can paste in some of the text that I have on the side. I've got mine copied over here. And I'm going to paste this in. Now I can see that I've got a pullquote here with some great information at the top of my page.

## Exploring the Block Editor Toolbar

Now that I've got my text in place, let me show you a few things about the block editor. Up here at the top, I can either choose the different type of block style. I can change the type of block that's in use. I can change the alignment if I want to align it to the left, to the right, to the middle, or go full width. I can also change some things about the text, if I want to go bold, italic, or add a hyperlink. I can also choose inline code, strikethrough, subscript, and a bunch of different text options here as well.

Now that my first block is set, I'll click out of this, and all we need to do is add a new block.

## Using the Columns and Image Blocks

Let's create another one by clicking on the plus sign again. Now let's look at some additional block features that we have. I've got six options here, but if I click browse all, you're going to see a bar open up on the left-hand side that has a ton of different options. I'm going to scroll down until I find the one I'm looking for, which is columns. Columns are one of my favorite types of blocks because they offer tons of different customization options.

As you can see, you have a bunch of different options here. I've got two columns, 50/50 width, 30/70, 70/30. Let's go with 50/50 for an even split. As you can see here, I've got two new blocks now. I've got one on the left and one on the right. Now, I think what would look great here are two images right next to each other.

On this left-hand side, I'm going to click the plus. Now I'm going to add an image block. Adding an image is easy because I can click upload here to upload a brand-new one, or I can go directly to my media library, or I can insert one from a URL that's already online.

I've got some stuff preloaded in my media library. Let's click there. I like this photo of my dog, Leah, so we'll click this one. And we'll click select. Now, I've got one image here.

I want to do the exact same thing on the right-hand side. I'm going to click that plus again. Click, image. Right back to my media library. Now, I'm going to choose a photo of me. Choose that one, click, select.

Now, I've got two images there and I think they look great.

## Adding Captions to Images

All I need to do now is click outside of either of these blocks. Now, again, hover over them, and click each individual block if I want to. Now, I can change the size, edit if I want to, and I want to add a caption down here at the bottom to give them some information about what this picture is.

I'll click in here, and to write caption, and I'll copy over some of this text that I've got. Do the same thing on the right-hand side. Paste that in.

Now, I've got two pictures right underneath that pullquote and I think they look great.

## Adding and Styling a Separator Block

Now, the next thing I want to do is start to add some design touches to this page. I want to break up the content a little bit so I'm going to add a new block. Click the plus sign here. The next thing I want to add is called a separator block. This is just that basic line that breaks up the text and the images on my page. As we can see here, just clicking it, I've got a new line that's added to the page.

If I want to extend this beyond the middle of the page, I can click this option here, change block type or style. We've got a wide line option or a dots option. I'm going to choose the wide line because that's going to stretch all the way across the page and I like the way that that looks.

## Duplicating and Moving Blocks on the Page

One of the things I like most about blocks is that they're super easy to move around the page. I really liked the way that this looks. Now, I want to add a new one. I'm going to click on this block here. Click these three dots for more options, and then I'm going to choose the duplicate option. Now, I just essentially made the same block twice.

Now, I'm going to click on this bottom one. Make sure it's highlighted. I'm going to choose this arrow that says move up. This essentially will allow me to move this up the page. As you can see, I'm slowly but surely moving it above all the other content. Now, I've got a separator block at the very top of my page, and I think that looks pretty nifty.

## Adding a Final Paragraph Block

Last but not least, let's head down to the bottom of the page and add some text to tell visitors a little bit more about who I am. We'll scroll down here and we're going to add, you guessed it, another block. I'll click here. This time, I'm going to add a paragraph. Now, that it's up, I'm going to paste in some of the text.

As I mentioned earlier, you can always play around with the text options here if you want to go bold or italic. I'm going to click out of that. Just scroll around and see how that looks. I think this looks pretty great so far.

## Publishing Your WordPress Page

Now, that we're done editing the page, the most important thing you can do is up here on the top right-hand corner, once you're done, click publish. Make sure that you do that or you can save it as a draft if you're not ready to take it live. Either way, make sure that you save your work before you get out of it.

I'll click publish. Before it allows you to publish, it's going to ask you to double-check a few of the settings here. The first thing it's going to ask you to look at is the visibility, so you can see if it's public, private, or password protected. I'm fine with this being public so we'll leave it as is. The next thing you can do is publish immediately. You can also choose down here if you want to schedule this page to be pushed on a certain date or time. I'm going to leave that to, immediately, for now, so we'll scroll back up to here and click publish.

At the bottom left-hand corner, you can see that the page is now live. I'm going to click, view page.

## Conclusion and What's Next

And here's my about page. Scroll down just a little bit. I think that looks pretty awesome. That's about it for creating a new page and adding content to it.

Stick around for our next video, where I'm going to show you how to make menus, widgets, and a whole lot more. As always, if you found this content helpful, please tell us in the comments below. Give it a like and subscribe if you want to see more. Thanks, y'all.
